title: DSA: graphs, BFS/DFS and topological sort
description: Graph representation, BFS and DFS, islands, clone graph, multi-source BFS, and Kahn's algorithm for topological order and cycle detection (course schedule).
source: LeetCode problem set and discuss; NeetCode roadmap; Cracking the Coding Interview; Oracle Java docs (ArrayDeque); Python docs (collections.deque, defaultdict, recursion limit)

questions.prompt: In the grid [[2,1,1],[1,1,0],[0,1,1]], 2 is a rotten orange, 1 is fresh, 0 is empty. Each minute, rot spreads to the 4 neighbours of every rotten orange. How many minutes until no fresh orange remains?
questions.explanation: Minute 1 rots (0,1) and (1,0); minute 2 rots (0,2) and (1,1); minute 3 rots (2,1); minute 4 rots (2,2). The answer is the number of BFS levels, 4. Starting the queue with all sources at once gives the distance to the nearest rotten orange in a single O(V + E) pass.

questions.prompt: Why enqueue every rotten orange at the start (distance 0) instead of running a separate BFS from each?

options.text: One BFS gives every cell its nearest-source distance.
options.why: Right: the frontier expands from all sources simultaneously, so the first arrival at a cell is the minimum over all sources.

options.text: It lets you swap the queue for a recursive DFS and keep the levels.
options.why: The method relies on queue order to get levels; DFS would not give shortest distances.

options.text: It is required to detect cycles in the grid before spreading.
options.why: Cycle detection is a different problem; this is about nearest distance.

options.text: It means you no longer need any visited marker anywhere in the grid.
options.why: You still need to mark cells as visited or they are re-queued.

questions.explanation: Multi-source BFS also solves "walls and gates", "01 matrix" and "distance to nearest 0".

questions.assertion: Graph DFS needs a visited set to terminate, whereas a tree DFS usually does not.
questions.reason: A graph can contain cycles, so you can return to a node you already explored.

whys.a: Correct: without marking, a cycle makes the traversal loop forever; a tree has no cycles.
whys.b: R is the direct reason, so "does not explain" is wrong.
whys.c: R is true, so this is wrong.
whys.d: A is true, so this is wrong.

questions.explanation: Mark nodes when you enqueue (BFS) or on entry (DFS) so each node is processed once, giving O(V + E).

questions.prompt: Evaluate the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: Plain BFS finds the cheapest path in a graph whose edges have different positive weights.
questions.reason: BFS visits nodes in increasing order of the number of edges from the source.

whys.a: A is false, so no explanation can hold.
whys.b: A is false, so both-true options cannot be right.
whys.c: R is true, so option c is wrong.
whys.d: Correct: BFS minimises the number of edges, not total weight, so use Dijkstra (priority queue) for weighted edges.

questions.explanation: BFS works for unit weights; 0-1 weights can use a deque (0-1 BFS); general non-negative weights need Dijkstra.

questions.prompt: Edges: 0->1, 1->2, 2->1, 2->3 (4 nodes). Kahn's algorithm starts with the nodes of in-degree 0. How many nodes does it leave unprocessed when it finishes?
questions.explanation: Only node 0 has in-degree 0; processing it lowers node 1 from 2 to 1, not 0, so the queue empties after one node. The 3 left over (1, 2, 3) include the cycle 1 -> 2 -> 1 and node 3 which depends on it.

questions.prompt: A DAG has edges 0->1, 0->2, 1->3, 2->3. How many different valid topological orders does it have?
questions.explanation: 0 must come first and 3 last; 1 and 2 can appear in either order: [0,1,2,3] and [0,2,1,3]. When Kahn's queue holds more than one node at once there are several valid orders.

questions.prompt: In clone graph, why keep a map from each original node to its copy?

options.text: It stops cycles and shared neighbours being copied twice.
options.why: Right: the map doubles as the visited set and ensures each node is copied exactly once with consistent links.

options.text: It lets you sort the neighbours before copying.
options.why: Neighbour order is preserved by the traversal; sorting is not needed.

options.text: It reduces memory because copies share the originals' neighbour lists.
options.why: A deep copy must not share nodes with the original graph.

options.text: It is only needed for directed graphs.
options.why: Undirected graphs always have cycles of length 2, so the map matters even more there.

questions.explanation: Without it, a cycle gives infinite recursion and shared neighbours get duplicated. BFS and DFS versions are both fine, O(V + E).

questions.prompt: Which statements about BFS on an unweighted graph are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: The first time BFS reaches a node is along a shortest path in number of edges.
options.why: Right: nodes are discovered level by level.

options.text: With an adjacency list it runs in O(V + E).
options.why: Right: each vertex is dequeued once and each edge examined a constant number of times.

options.text: The queue can hold at most the nodes of two adjacent levels at once.
options.why: Right: nodes of level d are dequeued while level d + 1 is enqueued.

options.text: It must use recursion, otherwise the visited set does not work.
options.why: BFS is iterative with an explicit queue; recursion is for DFS.

questions.explanation: BFS memory can be O(V) for a wide graph, DFS memory is O(depth); that trade-off is a standard follow-up.

questions.prompt: A recursive DFS over a path graph of 100,000 nodes will raise RecursionError in default CPython, so an explicit stack or raising the limit is needed.

options.why: Right: the default limit is 1000 frames, and a 100,000-deep chain exceeds it.
The default recursion limit is 1000, so deep graphs do fail.

questions.explanation: Use an iterative DFS with a list as a stack, or sys.setrecursionlimit with care (deep recursion can still crash the interpreter). Java has the same issue with StackOverflowError.
